clinicalPearls: A benign condition defined by the presence of ectopic glands lined by tubal-type ciliated epithelium outside the fallopian tube
Commonly found on the pelvic peritoneum, omentum, and within pelvic lymph nodes, and is usually an incidental histological finding
It is generally asymptomatic and discovered during surgery or histopathology performed for another indication
Psammoma bodies are frequently associated, which can cause confusion with serous neoplasia on cytology or histology
Unlike endometriosis, endosalpingiosis lacks endometrial stroma and haemosiderin, and is not associated with cyclical bleeding
Its main clinical importance lies in not being mistaken for a low-grade serous tumour or metastatic disease
No specific treatment is required once a confident benign diagnosis has been established
reference.pathophysiology: Endosalpingiosis consists of benign glands lined by the ciliated and secretory epithelium characteristic of the fallopian tube, situated in ectopic locations. It is thought to arise from the so-called secondary Müllerian system, whereby the pelvic mesothelium, which shares an embryological origin with the Müllerian ducts, undergoes metaplasia into tubal-type epithelium. Because the process produces glandular structures without endometrial stroma, it does not bleed cyclically as endometriosis does.
additionalDifferentials: Low-grade serous carcinoma or borderline serous tumour
additionalInvestigations: Histopathological examination, which is the basis of diagnosis
Careful review to distinguish benign glands from serous borderline or malignant lesions
Imaging, which is generally non-specific and used mainly to exclude other pathology
Serum CA-125, which may be mildly elevated and should be interpreted with caution
Correlation with the clinical and operative context
redFlags: Atypical or proliferative epithelial features raising the possibility of a serous borderline or malignant tumour
Coexisting serous neoplasia elsewhere in the pelvis
Unexpected nodal glandular tissue that could be misread as metastasis
Discordance between benign histology and clinical suspicion of malignancy
reference.prognosis: Endosalpingiosis is entirely benign with an excellent prognosis and generally requires no treatment; its significance is largely as a potential mimic of malignancy on histology.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing endosalpingiosis in lymph nodes as metastatic carcinoma
Confusing it with endometriosis despite the absence of stroma and haemosiderin
Misinterpreting associated psammoma bodies as evidence of malignancy
Instituting unnecessary treatment for an incidental benign finding
